articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions North Korean IT Worker Networks and Rwandan Ministry of Defence
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on 10 individuals and one entity involved in North Korean government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes. These schemes defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for North Korea's unlawful weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missile programs. The action aims to dismantle the infrastructure that converts fraudulent employment into illicit funding for Pyongyang's weapons development.

In a separate action, OFAC also designated the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and a financial institution for their support of the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This designation underscores the U.S. commitment to addressing destabilizing activities in the region.

These designations build on previous OFAC actions targeting DPRK IT worker networks and highlight a unified response from the United States, Australia, and the European Union to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation and revenue generation.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC Over Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to the public and regulated entities on compliance obligations.

The amendments are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to enhance transparency and assist U.S. persons in understanding and adhering to sanctions regulations. The updated FAQs cover various scenarios related to sanctions compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, General Licenses, and Delists Belarus and North Korea Entities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a new round of Iran-related designations as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting a network of legal, maritime, and shipping service providers facilitating Iran's sanctions evasion and petroleum trade. The action sanctioned five individuals, four entities, and nine vessels under Executive Order 13902.

In connection with these designations, OFAC issued Iran-related General Licenses (GL) GG and HH, authorizing certain wind-down activities through November 20, 2026. GL HH specifically authorizes the wind down of transactions involving Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A. and its blocked vessels.

Additionally, OFAC removed two individuals and two entities from the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs. The delisted entities include Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov and Chinese national Lu Hezheng, along with two China-based animation studios.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

OFAC issued two new PAIPA-related General Licenses: GL 1, which generally authorizes transactions prohibited under PAIPA to the extent they are authorized or exempt under the Cyber-related Sanctions Regulations, and GL 2, which authorizes wind-down activities for certain designated entities through January 19, 2027.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The amendment, GL 60A, extends the authorization for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.

GL 60A replaces and supersedes GL 60, extending the authorization period from its original end date of October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027. This extension aims to facilitate ongoing humanitarian and reconstruction efforts in the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Cuba Entity, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities for allegedly enabling sanctions evasion and sustaining Iran's military and proxy forces. The designated parties include Iran-based banks Jazireh International Bank Company and Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company, which OFAC stated operated offshore in free trade zones.

In a separate action, OFAC also designated an entity related to Cuba. This designation comes amidst ongoing efforts to implement Executive Order 14404, which imposes sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba.
Accompanying these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on the scope of the new restrictions and authorized activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Prominent Venezuelan Politician Jorge Rodriguez from SDN List
body: The U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Rodriguez, a prominent Venezuelan political figure, from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) list. This action lifts the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons engaging with him.

Rodriguez, who serves as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, was initially designated in 2018. His delisting is part of Washington's latest diplomatic efforts and a push for expanded energy investment in Venezuela.

While this represents a significant easing of sanctions on an individual, broader 2017 sanctions and 2019 blocking sanctions against the Venezuelan government largely remain in place. Most sanctions relief has been in the form of General Licenses, which OFAC can revoke or modify.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks supporting such operations globally.
The designations underscore OFAC's commitment to combating international drug trafficking and terrorist financing by imposing financial restrictions on those who facilitate these illicit activities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has entered into a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The settlement amount is $11,662,930.

This settlement is part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), highlighting a multi-agency approach to addressing compliance failures within financial institutions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Designating 1,569 Individuals and Entities
body: The European Union has adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to its sanctions lists. This brings the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The new listings, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including companies involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

This package, implemented through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2279 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2281, emphasizes additional designations and asset freezes rather than new trade or financial restrictions.

articles.headline: EU Adds Three Individuals and Four Entities to DPRK Sanctions List
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations target those responsible for supporting DPRK's nuclear and missile programs and for violating UN sanctions.

The new listings are linked to growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia and 'arms-for-oil' trade, which are in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

The EU reaffirms its commitment to the full implementation of UN sanctions against the DPRK and calls on Pyongyang to abandon its WMD and ballistic missile programs in a complete, verifiable, and irreversible manner.

articles.headline: UK Designates Two Individuals Under Iran Sanctions Regime for Hostile Activity
body: The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has updated the UK Sanctions List with two additions under The Iran (Sanctions) Regulations 2023. The designated individuals are Ruhollah BAZGHANDI and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh JAKKI.

BAZGHANDI is suspected of involvement in hostile activity by the Government of Iran, including planning or conducting espionage. JAKKI is suspected of involvement in hostile activity by the Government of Iran through supporting or assisting in threatening, planning, or conducting attacks against persons in countries other than Iran.
These designations impose asset freezes, travel bans, and director disqualification sanctions on both individuals, underscoring the UK's commitment to countering Iranian hostile activities.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends Three Entries on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On October 26, 2026, the UN Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted amendments to three entries on its ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

These amendments involve updates to identifying information for listed individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo. The updated list is accessible on the Committee's website.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

articles.headline: OFAC Alerts Foreign Financial Institutions to Sanctions Risk for Business with Iran
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an alert to foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that continue to do business with Iran or its financial sector. The alert warns that these institutions may be sanctioned under 'Operation Economic Outcast.'

OFAC emphasizes that FFIs transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should immediately terminate such activities and relationships. This follows Treasury's expansion of secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13902 for entities supporting Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping sectors.

Previous actions under 'Operation Economic Outcast' include severing U.S. correspondent banking access for Banque Misr UAE, designating Türkiye-based Golden Global Bank for facilitating transactions for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force, and designating VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company for involvement in Iranian sanctions evasion.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Cuba Sanctions Regulations and Amends Existing CACR
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new Cuba Sanctions Regulations (CSR) at 31 C.F.R. Part 516, effective September 30, 2026. These new regulations fully implement Executive Order (EO) 14404, 'Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and Threats to United States National Security and Foreign Policy,' signed by President Trump in May 2026.

The CSR establish a new, separate sanctions program and allow for sanctions against foreign financial institutions that conduct or facilitate significant transactions for or on behalf of any person whose property is blocked by these sanctions. OFAC also amended the existing Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) at 31 C.F.R. Part 515.

Revisions to the CACR include a new prohibition on indirect financial transactions with entities on the Cuba Restricted List and narrowed authorizations for certain travel-related transactions. Educational travel now requires sponsorship by a U.S. organization and accompaniment by a representative, and professional meeting travel to Cuba requires a specific OFAC license.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Holland & Knight / Thompson Hine LLP

articles.headline: U.S. Consumer Confidence Rebounds in October as Gas Prices Ease
body: American consumer confidence in the economy rebounded somewhat in October, primarily due to a modest easing of gas prices, although they remain elevated. This recovery follows a period of declining sentiment.

Despite the improved consumer outlook, CEO confidence moved back into negative territory in the fourth quarter, revealing contrasting perspectives on the U.S. economic outlook. Consumers generally feel their household income should be higher in six months, indicating a degree of optimism about their personal financial situations.

Businesses, however, are flagging geopolitical uncertainty, alongside AI and cyber issues, as key concerns. While CEOs hope for increased productivity from AI investments, they are also tracking the inherent risks of new technologies.

articles.headline: UN General Assembly Condemns U.S. Embargo on Cuba for 34th Consecutive Year
body: The United Nations General Assembly has overwhelmingly adopted a resolution condemning the U.S. economic, trade, and financial embargo against Cuba for the 34th consecutive year. The resolution, drafted by Cuba, was supported by 130 states, with 17 voting against and 25 abstaining.

Despite the strong international condemnation, the resolution is recommendatory and does not alter U.S. rules on travel, trade, or money transfers. The number of votes in favor of the resolution decreased by 35 compared to 2025, marking the lowest support since 1995.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, urged states to vote against the document, stating that the U.S. does not impose a blockade and highlighting significant U.S. exports to Cuba. However, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla criticized the U.S. measures as collective punishment.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties for BSA Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, detailing various penalties against financial institutions and institution-affiliated parties. These actions are taken to deter violations, encourage correction of unsafe or unsound practices, and prevent breaches of fiduciary duty.

Among the actions, the OCC issued a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs.

Additionally, the OCC imposed a Civil Money Penalty of $750 million against Bank of America, National Association, for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, including failure to timely file suspicious activity reports and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. Prohibition Orders were also issued against individuals for embezzling customer funds.

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has assessed a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its willful failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

This FinCEN penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action, with FinCEN crediting $750 million of its assessment against a concurrent civil money penalty imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for the bank's deficient BSA/AML compliance program. Additionally, OFAC announced an $11.6 million settlement with the bank for sanctions violations.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
